scope: Prepare before ordinary sick days or an explicitly mentioned planned recovery. Care access and everyday logistics, not clinical decisions or emergency response.
provenance: Assistant-authored, researched candidates. Not live catalog entries, professionally reviewed advice or recorded OpenAI API outputs. Textual fit rules require implementation before automated selection.
question: What would you like to have figured out before a sick day?
helper_text: Choose what matters to you. We'll start with a few useful options.

concerns.label: Where to get care, and what it might cost
Getting food, prescriptions and everyday essentials
Making things easier at home while I rest
Having my pet cared for if I can't do the usual routine
Keeping work or study manageable if I need time off
Finding practical help or someone to check in with

manual_input.label: Anything specific you'd like help with?
manual_input.placeholder: For example: I have a cat, no nearby help, and want to prepare without booking anything yet.

tasks.title: Find a care option you can actually start with
tasks.summary: You don't need a regular doctor to explore your options. Start with one route that fits your coverage and budget.
steps: With insurance, look for virtual care in your plan or benefits portal. Without a suitable benefit, try HRSA's health-center finder.
Ask one service: 'Can a new patient in my state have a virtual first visit, and what would it cost?'
Check how to request that first visit. Keep the entry page and the answer; if you contacted the service, wait for its reply.
tasks.done_when: One first-visit route has confirmed new-patient access and cost information. An unanswered inquiry is still pending.
tasks.use_when: She wants an initial care route and has not already established a suitable one. US service variant only.
tasks.skip_when: A suitable care route already exists, or the current request asks for symptom assessment or immediate care.
tasks.new_value: Discover an entry point without presuming an existing doctor; learn whether it is usable before relying on it.
tasks.cost: Research only; future care may cost money. No account, booking or subscription required by this task.
tasks.variants: If explicitly interested in self-pay virtual care, use a reviewed pay-per-visit provider and check current first-patient eligibility and total cost. If uninsured and cost-sensitive, start with the health center. These are variants of one outcome, not extra tasks.
tasks.waiting: Provider reply if details are not published.

tasks.title: Know where an in-person visit could start
tasks.summary: An online option doesn't answer every access question. If you want an in-person route too, check one clinic before you need it.
steps: Use your insurer's provider directory, or HRSA's finder without suitable coverage, to locate a nearby clinic accepting new patients.
Check whether first visits need advance registration and whether appointments or walk-ins are offered. Ask about your likely visit charge.
Confirm the clinic's address and booking route directly. Leave questions pending until answered; you don't need to book today.
tasks.done_when: You know one clinic's new-patient process, location and cost information for a future nonurgent visit.
tasks.use_when: She explicitly wants an in-person route and lacks one, or has an established virtual route with an identified in-person access gap.
tasks.skip_when: Her existing clinic already meets this need. Do not add alongside SC01 merely to fill a batch.
tasks.new_value: Find out whether a clinic can actually accept her, rather than treating a map result as access.
tasks.cost: Research free; appointment costs vary.
tasks.variants: For insured users, replace the finder with their own plan directory. No AI judgment about which symptoms belong at which facility.
tasks.waiting: Clinic or insurer reply.

tasks.title: Try the doorway to your first video visit
tasks.summary: Finding care is one piece; being able to connect is another. A short practice now can uncover the awkward bits.
steps: Open your chosen provider's joining instructions. Find its practice or device-check option without starting a paid consultation.
Try the camera and sound from a private spot. If video, captions or another feature doesn't work for you, contact support.
Ask how to reconnect or whether an appropriate phone alternative exists. Keep the provider's technical-help route with your visit link.
tasks.done_when: You have tested the connection and know whom to contact if it fails; any needed accessibility arrangement is confirmed.
tasks.use_when: A chosen virtual provider exists and the person has not successfully used its setup, or reports an access barrier.
tasks.skip_when: She already uses this setup successfully. No new app installation or paid visit just for a test.
tasks.new_value: Discover first-use technology or accessibility barriers while there is time to resolve them.
tasks.cost: No purchase; use an existing device.
tasks.waiting: Support reply if a test or accommodation is needed.

tasks.title: Find a way to an appointment without driving
tasks.summary: Some transport options need advance notice. Find out what you could use before the day you need a ride.
steps: If you have Medicaid, ask your plan about nonemergency medical transport. Otherwise, ask the clinic or local 211 about suitable transport options.
Ask one provider about eligibility, booking notice and the full return-trip cost. Mention any access assistance you actually need.
Check how the journey home is arranged, especially if the appointment runs late. Keep a confirmed booking route; don't reserve a trip yet.
tasks.done_when: You have an eligible transport option with confirmed booking and return-trip details. An unanswered inquiry is still pending.
tasks.use_when: She identifies a nonurgent appointment-transport gap. Medicaid route requires confirmed enrollment; local 211 route is US-specific.
tasks.skip_when: Transport is already arranged, she needs emergency transport, or this is an escort requirement after a procedure.
tasks.new_value: Discover possible transport assistance and its advance-booking and return-trip conditions.
tasks.cost: Research free; eligibility and ride charges vary. Do not promise free rides.
tasks.waiting: Transport-provider eligibility confirmation.

tasks.title: Check what 'someone to take you home' really means
tasks.summary: For a planned procedure, a ride and an approved escort can be different things. Let the clinic explain what your appointment requires.
steps: Ask your procedure team who may accompany you home and whether someone must stay afterward. Use their instructions for your appointment.
If you have no suitable person, say so now. Ask the clinic's coordinator about acceptable arrangements and any referral or cost information.
Have the team confirm that your proposed arrangement meets its requirements before relying on it. Keep unresolved care needs with the team.
tasks.done_when: Your procedure team has confirmed an acceptable arrangement. An unresolved gap or a ride booking alone isn't completion.
tasks.use_when: She explicitly mentions a planned procedure or recovery with a possible escort requirement.
tasks.skip_when: Ordinary sick-day preparation with no planned procedure. Never infer a procedure from living alone.
tasks.new_value: Learn an easily missed requirement before an appointment is disrupted; access the clinic's coordination help.
tasks.cost: Planning free; acceptable transport or support may cost money.
tasks.waiting: Clinical team and prospective escort confirmation.

tasks.title: Ask what your planned visit will actually cost
tasks.summary: A headline consultation price may not cover everything. For a planned self-pay visit, you can ask for a written estimate.
steps: For US care you won't pay for through insurance, ask the provider about a written 'good faith estimate' before the planned visit.
Ask whether it includes facility charges or likely separate services. If another provider bills separately, ask that provider for its estimate too.
Read the answers before deciding about the visit. Keep the estimate privately and ask about any charge you still don't understand.
tasks.done_when: You have the estimate and understand what it includes; a request without an answer remains pending.
tasks.use_when: A specific nonemergency US visit is being planned and the person will not use insurance to pay.
tasks.skip_when: She is only exploring care generally, using insurance, or seeking emergency care. Do not suggest delaying needed care for an estimate.
tasks.new_value: Learn a concrete way to clarify planned care costs, beyond saving a provider's advertised starting price.
tasks.cost: No purchase or booking required to ask.
tasks.waiting: Written estimate from each relevant provider.

tasks.title: Find out whether a pharmacy can reach your door
tasks.summary: A new prescription and a routine mail-order refill can have different delivery arrangements. Check the route you might actually need.
steps: Choose a local pharmacy from your plan's directory, if insured, or an official pharmacy site. You don't need an existing prescription today.
Ask whether eligible new prescriptions can be delivered to your area, the cutoff time after they're ready, and the full delivery charge.
Check how delivery is requested and received. Keep the route if workable; confirm eligibility for any actual prescription with the pharmacy later.
tasks.done_when: You understand the pharmacy's delivery process and restrictions. Eligibility for an actual future prescription still needs checking.
tasks.use_when: She lacks a workable prescription-acquisition route or asks specifically about delivery. US linked example only.
tasks.skip_when: Delivery already works for her, or she asks which medication to obtain.
tasks.new_value: Discover local prescription delivery without assuming a regular pharmacy, and distinguish it from slower refill shipping.
tasks.cost: Research only; delivery and prescriptions may cost money.
tasks.waiting: Pharmacy response; no ordering or transfers now.

tasks.title: Find out what could hold up your next refill
tasks.summary: If you already use a regular prescription, a refill request may need more than a tap in an app. Ask before you're close to running out.
steps: Ask your pharmacist how your usual refill process works and whether a prescriber renewal or other approval is needed next time.
Ask when they recommend starting the request and whom to contact if it stalls, including before a holiday closure.
Set a private reminder using that advice. Keep your prescribed routine unchanged; let the pharmacist or prescriber handle medication decisions.
tasks.done_when: You know the next refill's process and lead time, with a reminder based on professional guidance.
tasks.use_when: She explicitly reports an ongoing prescription and uncertainty or previous delays in getting refills.
tasks.skip_when: No ongoing prescription is known, or the refill process is already reliable. An immediate missed-dose question requires professional advice.
tasks.new_value: Uncover administrative lead times before a supply gap; delivery setup alone does not solve renewal delays.
tasks.cost: No purchase or extra medicine requested.
tasks.waiting: Pharmacist or prescriber reply. Do not store medication details in My Safety.

tasks.title: Check whether someone else can collect for you
tasks.summary: If delivery won't work, a willing person may be able to collect a prescription. Check the pharmacy's process before either of you makes a trip.
steps: Ask your pharmacy what it requires when someone else collects on your behalf, including identification, payment and any prescription-specific restrictions.
Ask a person you already trust whether this is help they could offer. Explain the process without sharing account passwords.
Agree how you would request a pickup and share only the details the pharmacy needs, privately, when a real collection is arranged.
tasks.done_when: The pharmacy has explained its process and a willing person understands how a future collection would work.
tasks.use_when: A trusted willing local contact exists and pharmacy collection is an identified gap, especially when delivery is unsuitable.
tasks.skip_when: No suitable contact, acquisition already works, or she wants to send an unverified stranger for medication.
tasks.new_value: Resolve a practical permission and logistics question rather than assuming another person can simply show up.
tasks.cost: Planning free; prescription charges remain separate.
tasks.waiting: Both pharmacy answer and helper agreement.

tasks.title: See whether groceries can reach your actual door
tasks.summary: Delivery coverage is only the start. The useful question is whether the cost and handoff would work on a day you need rest.
steps: Check your usual grocer's delivery page for your address. If it doesn't deliver, inspect one local alternative without buying a membership.
Preview a realistic small order. Check the final fees and minimum, then confirm whether the handoff is at your door or building entrance.
Check what happens when an essential item is unavailable. Save a workable option or ask support to resolve the specific obstacle; don't check out.
tasks.done_when: You understand one service's total order cost, delivery location and substitution options well enough to decide whether it fits.
tasks.use_when: Grocery delivery is untested or there is an explicit cost, access or substitution problem.
tasks.skip_when: She already has a reliable suitable service. If no-spend includes future paid services, prefer SC11 or an agreed existing helper.
tasks.new_value: Expose minimum-order charges, building handoffs and substitutions before relying on delivery.
tasks.cost: No test purchase; future food and service costs must fit her budget.
tasks.variants: If she explicitly uses EBT, explain that provider fees may need another payment method and inspect that service's current terms. Do not collect benefit information just to personalize.
tasks.waiting: Support reply if the delivery location or fees are unclear.

tasks.title: Find food help without a delivery budget
tasks.summary: When food costs are the obstacle, another shopping app may not help. A local food program is a different route worth checking.
steps: Use Feeding America's finder to reach your local food bank and ask about a nearby pantry or meal program for temporary help.
Check who can use it, opening times and what a first visit requires. Say if transport or collecting food is the obstacle.
Ask whether delivery or collection by someone else is available there. Keep the confirmed access route; if it doesn't fit, ask for another referral.
tasks.done_when: You have a confirmed local food option and a workable way to receive it. Unanswered referrals are still pending.
tasks.use_when: She explicitly identifies food affordability or lack of paid-delivery access. US only for the linked route.
tasks.skip_when: No affordability/access concern is expressed. Do not infer financial hardship from living alone or lack of insurance.
tasks.new_value: Discover temporary community food support and check whether she could actually receive it.
tasks.cost: Directory research free; program terms vary. Do not promise free home delivery.
tasks.waiting: Local program reply. No eligibility promise.

tasks.title: Give one easy meal a real-life try
tasks.summary: 'Easy' can still mean thawing, chopping or finding a missing ingredient. Try a meal while you have the energy to spot those catches.
steps: Choose a familiar meal you'd want with little effort. Include a no-cook option if cooking is the part you want to avoid.
Make it during a normal mealtime. Notice packaging, tools, extra ingredients and cleanup; swap the part that makes it harder than expected.
Keep the ingredients available within their storage instructions and your budget. Put anything missing on your next usual shop, rather than buying a special kit.
tasks.done_when: You have tried the meal and its ingredients are available. A shopping note alone means it is not ready yet.
tasks.use_when: She lacks a tested low-effort meal, or her current options have a specific preparation barrier.
tasks.skip_when: Suitable meals are already prepared. Avoid turning this into generic nutrition or treatment advice.
tasks.new_value: A practical rehearsal exposes hidden effort; this is not another list of foods she already eats.
tasks.cost: Use a normal meal and existing food; replacing missing ingredients may cost money.
tasks.variants: A freezer meal is an alternative within this outcome, not a second task called 'prepare soup'. No dietary prescriptions.
tasks.waiting: Cooking/storage time is additional to active effort.

tasks.title: Make your resting spot work for you
tasks.summary: Try the setup from where you'll actually sit or lie down. You'll notice more than you do while standing beside it.
steps: Sit in your usual resting spot and try reaching your drink, tissues and phone. Test the charger from that position.
Move what you keep getting up for onto an existing stable surface. Keep liquids away from electrical equipment and cables out of walkways.
Try it again, including getting up normally. Keep only changes that make reaching things and moving around easier.
tasks.done_when: Your chosen essentials are reachable and the setup leaves a clear way through.
tasks.use_when: She reports repeated getting up, awkward reach or an unsuitable resting space, or explicitly wants a simple physical preparation.
tasks.skip_when: The setup already works. Do not use this familiar task as the default for someone asking for overlooked services.
tasks.new_value: Test usability rather than collecting more objects or purchasing an emergency basket.
tasks.cost: No purchase; rearrange existing ordinary items.
tasks.waiting: None.

tasks.title: Take one last-minute shop off your future plate
tasks.summary: Think of the everyday item that has actually sent you out at an inconvenient time. Prepare for that gap, instead of buying a generic sick-day kit.
steps: Pick a nonmedical essential you regularly use and have run out of, such as tissues, menstrual products or pet litter.
Check what you have and its storage instructions. If useful and affordable, add a modest spare to your next normal shop.
Place the spare where you'll use it and add a replacement to your shopping list when you open it. Use your existing system.
tasks.done_when: That specific supply gap is covered and you have a simple cue to replace it when used.
tasks.use_when: She describes a recurring shortage or explicitly wants material preparation; the item must come from her own routine.
tasks.skip_when: Adequate supplies already exist, buying anything is not feasible, or the request concerns medication quantities.
tasks.new_value: Close an actual recurring shortage rather than prescribe a stockpile. Lower priority for users seeking unfamiliar options.
tasks.cost: May require a routine purchase; never recommend stockpiling or automatic subscriptions.
tasks.waiting: Next ordinary shop, if needed.

tasks.title: Check how your go-to meal keeps
tasks.summary: This is useful if food you set aside has spoiled or left you guessing. Learn the storage guidance for one meal you actually use.
steps: Choose the food that leaves you unsure about storage. Read its packaging and look up the matching food in USDA's FoodKeeper.
Check guidance for your situation: unopened, opened or cooked. Follow the product's instructions and official guidance; don't judge safety by smell alone.
Use that guidance for the next portion you prepare or open. If you freeze it, label what it is and when it was prepared.
tasks.done_when: You understand the relevant storage instructions and have applied them to your next portion.
tasks.use_when: She reports uncertainty or waste around an existing prepared food. The exact food and storage circumstances must be known to her.
tasks.skip_when: Storage already works or she wants a general sick-day starting task. Don't assess whether a particular questionable food is safe through AI.
tasks.new_value: A reusable food-storage reference and a specific skill; not another meal-preparation card.
tasks.cost: No purchase.
tasks.waiting: Apply at the next normal meal; elapsed time may span days.

tasks.title: Let laundry leave the house without you
tasks.summary: If carrying laundry is the hard part, wash-and-fold pickup may be more useful than another household checklist.
steps: Check a local laundromat's pickup service or Taskrabbit laundry help for your area. Look for the work you need, not a recurring plan.
Ask about minimum charges, pickup location and return time. Check any detergent needs and which items the service will not accept.
Confirm whether you must be present or supply anything. Keep one workable option; no booking or payment needed now.
tasks.done_when: You know one service's handoff, return time, total charging method and relevant restrictions.
tasks.use_when: Laundry access is an expressed burden and future paid help is within her stated preferences.
tasks.skip_when: Laundry is already covered or paid services are ruled out. Do not treat contaminated laundry as an ordinary service order.
tasks.new_value: Discover a service that removes transport and lifting, including the handoff and minimum-charge details.
tasks.cost: Research free; future service paid. Compare minimum total, not hourly rate alone.
tasks.waiting: Provider response.

tasks.title: Price the cleaning help you'd actually want
tasks.summary: You may want the dishes and bathroom handled, not a whole-house deep clean. Find out whether a small, specific visit is possible.
steps: Choose one or two chores you would want help with. Compare a local cleaner's service page with one Taskrabbit listing if available.
Ask about the minimum booking, supplies and full charge for that scope. Check cancellation and household-illness policies before planning a visit.
Decide whether the service and cost fit. Keep a suitable candidate and the agreed scope; don't book or share access details yet.
tasks.done_when: A candidate has answered your scope and price questions, so you can decide whether the service fits.
tasks.use_when: Specific household work is the concern and researching paid help is welcome.
tasks.skip_when: No practical cleaning gap, paid help is excluded, or the need is medical/personal care rather than ordinary cleaning.
tasks.new_value: Discover whether a limited job is available and worthwhile, rather than assuming a full cleaning package is necessary.
tasks.cost: Research free; future paid minimum may make a small job unsuitable.
tasks.waiting: Cleaner reply. Follow the provider's illness policy.

tasks.title: Find help for an errand you can't postpone
tasks.summary: Some errands fall outside grocery delivery. Start with the exact job, then look for a service or local program that handles it.
steps: Choose one nonmedical errand, such as collecting a repaired item. For paid help, try Taskrabbit; for community options, contact local 211.
Ask about that exact job, area, notice and total charges. If collection is involved, check the shop's permission or identification requirements.
Keep one suitable contact and its booking process. If no service fits, leave the gap open rather than treating a directory as arranged help.
tasks.done_when: A provider has confirmed it can handle that kind of errand and explained how you would arrange it.
tasks.use_when: An identified nonmedical errand needs outside help. Choose the paid or community route from her preferences; linked coverage is US-first.
tasks.skip_when: The errand already has a solution, it is medication collection, or she needs hands-on personal care.
tasks.new_value: Convert an overlooked errand into a checked service option without assuming nearby friends.
tasks.cost: Research free; paid and community routes have different terms. A referral is not a guarantee of free assistance.
tasks.waiting: Service or referral response.

tasks.title: Make a check-in something you both want
tasks.summary: A short chat can be welcome without becoming another obligation. Set it up with someone you already feel comfortable asking.
steps: Choose a person you'd like to hear from on a sick day. They don't need to live nearby.
Ask what would suit you both: a message, short call or voice note, and a reasonable time. Make declining or rescheduling easy.
Agree how you'd ask for a check-in and let each other know if plans change. Keep it flexible.
tasks.done_when: You both agree on a comfortable way to arrange a check-in; an unanswered message is still pending.
tasks.use_when: She wants companionship and has named or confirmed a trusted person she is comfortable asking.
tasks.skip_when: She prefers quiet, has no such contact, or wants emergency monitoring. Living alone is not evidence of loneliness.
tasks.new_value: An actual mutual arrangement that respects both people's preferences, not a contact list or assumed availability.
tasks.cost: No purchase.
tasks.waiting: The other person's reply.

tasks.title: Turn 'let me know' into one easy-to-ask favor
tasks.summary: This is for someone who has already offered help. Make one practical arrangement so neither of you has to guess later.
steps: Choose a concrete favor within their offer, such as adding your groceries to an errand they're already doing.
Ask when it might work, how much notice they need and how payment or reimbursement would be handled. Leave room for a no.
Agree how you would request that favor and arrange a handoff. Keep it flexible; a past offer doesn't guarantee help on every date.
tasks.done_when: You have a mutually agreed way to request one practical favor, including timing and any costs.
tasks.use_when: A suitable trusted person has offered practical help and the user wants to clarify it.
tasks.skip_when: No available trusted helper, she dislikes asking this person, or the same errand has already been arranged.
tasks.new_value: Resolve what an existing offer actually means; not a generic request-writing exercise for someone without support.
tasks.cost: Favor may be free; purchases and reimbursement must be agreed.
tasks.waiting: Mutual agreement.

tasks.title: Find something a faraway person could help with
tasks.summary: Distance rules out dropping by, but it doesn't rule out practical help. Pick something useful that doesn't require access to your accounts.
steps: Choose a trusted person who wants to help and one remote job, such as researching a laundry service or comparing appointment transport options.
Agree what they would check and when they'd send the result. Keep final booking, spending and provider decisions with you unless explicitly agreed.
Try the handoff while you're well using a real small question. Share only what they need; keep passwords and medical details private.
tasks.done_when: You have tried one remote handoff and know what this person is comfortable helping with in future.
tasks.use_when: She has a willing trusted distant contact and wants practical help, rather than only a social check-in.
tasks.skip_when: No willing contact, delegation isn't wanted, or the useful work is already done. Do not create artificial research just to practice.
tasks.new_value: Make distant support practical through a real, bounded handoff; preserve the user's decisions and privacy.
tasks.cost: No purchase for the handoff.
tasks.waiting: The other person's availability and result.

tasks.title: Find the simplest way to take a sick day
tasks.summary: Knowing the reporting process beforehand can remove a decision when you're tired. Check the rules that actually apply to your work or course.
steps: Open your workplace policy or course guidance. Find whom to notify, the required channel and when notice is expected.
If unclear, ask the responsible office about the process and any required documentation. Don't assume paid leave or a particular entitlement.
Save a short ready-to-adapt message with only required details. For example: 'I'm unwell and need to be absent today. Please confirm the next step.'
tasks.done_when: The applicable absence process is clear and your message is ready to adapt.
tasks.use_when: She works or studies, doesn't know the reporting process and wants to reduce that friction.
tasks.skip_when: She already knows the process or works for herself without an employer/course. Legal eligibility questions need jurisdiction-specific guidance.
tasks.new_value: Discover the actual notice and documentation requirements; the message is a useful byproduct, not the whole task.
tasks.cost: No purchase. This does not promise paid time off.
tasks.waiting: Workplace or course-office reply if unclear.

tasks.title: Make one work handoff usable without you
tasks.summary: Pick the responsibility that really keeps pulling you back in. A tiny tested handoff is more useful than a long document nobody can use.
steps: With your manager or teammate, choose one time-sensitive duty they can appropriately cover and confirm that they agree to take it.
Put its next action, authorized file location and decision contact in your work system. Use approved access permissions, never shared passwords.
Ask them to open the handoff and explain what they'd do first. Fix the missing information their attempt reveals.
tasks.done_when: An agreed cover person can access and use the handoff for that duty.
tasks.use_when: She has a real time-sensitive work responsibility, authorized cover is possible, and absence is difficult because information depends on her.
tasks.skip_when: No teammate or authorized cover exists, or her work is already covered. Do not pressure her to keep working while ill.
tasks.new_value: Test someone else's ability to act, rather than writing a vague absence note or duplicating known work information.
tasks.cost: No purchase.
tasks.waiting: Colleague agreement and short trial. Keep business information out of My Safety.

tasks.title: Find the pause button for your own business
tasks.summary: If new orders or bookings keep arriving when you're unavailable, learn what your actual platform can pause—and what still needs attention.
steps: Open the official help for your shop or booking platform. Look for vacation mode, booking availability or temporary closure.
Check whether it pauses only new work, and what happens to existing commitments, recurring fees and messages. Don't change live settings today.
Draft a customer notice and a short plan for existing commitments. Keep the official instructions ready for a future decision to pause.
tasks.done_when: You know the platform's actual pause behavior and have a plan for commitments it doesn't pause.
tasks.use_when: She runs a solo business through a named platform and needs a way to handle temporary unavailability.
tasks.skip_when: No business/platform is known, or this process already exists. No tool action to close a real shop is authorized by this preparation task.
tasks.new_value: Discover that pausing incoming work may leave existing orders and fees active; prepare for the actual limits.
tasks.cost: Research free; existing business fees may continue during a future pause.
tasks.variants: Attach ETSY_PAUSE only for an Etsy seller; another platform needs its own reviewed official instructions, not guessed controls.
tasks.waiting: None for preparation. This task never changes live business settings.

tasks.title: Look for practical care help in your work benefits
tasks.summary: Some employers offer care support beyond health insurance. It is worth checking the actual benefit before paying for help yourself.
steps: Search your benefits portal for care support, dependent care or pet care. If nothing is clear, ask benefits support whether such assistance exists.
Describe the practical situation you want to prepare for. Ask whether it qualifies, what you pay and whether advance registration is needed.
Keep the official claim or booking instructions if eligible. If the benefit doesn't cover your situation, mark that route as unsuitable.
tasks.done_when: You know whether your employer's benefit fits your situation, and how to use it if eligible.
tasks.use_when: She has employer benefits and an unresolved practical-care responsibility. Do not infer benefits from employment alone.
tasks.skip_when: No employer benefit, already checked, or no relevant care need. Many programs support working employees during care disruptions; personal sick leave may not qualify.
tasks.new_value: Discover a potentially overlooked subsidized service and check the specific restrictions before assuming coverage.
tasks.cost: Research free; employer-specific copays, limits and registration may apply.
tasks.waiting: Benefits administrator reply. No promise that a branded provider is included.

tasks.title: Find care that fits your kind of pet
tasks.summary: A nearby listing is a starting point. Find out whether the person can handle your pet's routine and how future visits would be arranged.
steps: Use PSI's sitter finder to locate one business serving your area and pet type. Check its experience and service details.
Ask about notice, total visit cost and any introductory meeting. Mention the routine you need help with, without sending home-access details.
Read the reply and decide whether to arrange an introduction. A good candidate is worth keeping; it isn't a confirmed future booking.
tasks.done_when: One candidate has answered your practical questions and you can decide whether to meet them.
tasks.use_when: She has a pet, lacks suitable care and is open to researching paid help. Resource coverage must match her country/area.
tasks.skip_when: No pet is known, a suitable carer already exists, or paid care is not feasible.
tasks.new_value: Learn service fit and first-use requirements before a pet-care need arises.
tasks.cost: Research free; introductions and visits may carry charges. Ask first.
tasks.waiting: Candidate reply. Directory membership is not an endorsement.

tasks.title: Try the pet-care handoff together
tasks.summary: A real walkthrough can reveal the detail a feeding note misses. Use it to decide whether the arrangement works for both you and your pet.
steps: Arrange an introduction with a candidate you've chosen, confirming any charge first. Stay present while they meet your pet.
Show the ordinary routine and ask them to walk through it. Capture only the details they need, including who to contact with questions.
Resolve unclear instructions and discuss how visits would be requested if you're ill, including what happens if the carer becomes unavailable.
tasks.done_when: You've met, checked the routine together and decided whether this carer fits. Future dates still need agreement.
tasks.use_when: A suitable candidate exists and an introductory visit has not happened. The user wants to take that next step.
tasks.skip_when: A trusted carer already knows the routine. Do not repeat an existing feeding note; address only a remaining handoff gap.
tasks.new_value: Move from a listing to observed practical fit; make instructions usable by another person.
tasks.cost: Meeting or trial charges may apply; ask before arranging.
tasks.waiting: Scheduling and meeting time; travel additional. Never store access codes in My Safety.

tasks.title: Ask your vet what a pet carer would need
tasks.summary: Knowing the vet's number may not be the whole arrangement. Ask how they handle a carer's call when you aren't available.
steps: Ask your vet what permission or paperwork they use when someone else brings your pet for care and you can't immediately answer.
Discuss the decisions and payment arrangements you are comfortable authorizing. Use the practice's process rather than an AI-written legal form.
Share the agreed process with your chosen carer through a private channel, and confirm the practice has what it needs.
tasks.done_when: Your vet and chosen carer understand the permission and contact process you have agreed.
tasks.use_when: A pet and chosen carer exist, and veterinary permission during the user's absence is an unresolved concern.
tasks.skip_when: This is already arranged or the pet needs medical advice now. Do not suggest blanket authorization or unlimited spending.
tasks.new_value: Discover an administrative gap that a phone number or feeding note alone does not cover.
tasks.cost: Administrative preparation; ask about any charge. No treatment authorized by this app.
tasks.waiting: Vet-practice confirmation. Keep permissions and payment details outside My Safety.

tasks.title: Explore temporary pet care when paid sitting won't stretch
tasks.summary: For an expected longer absence, some communities have temporary foster support for owned pets. Find out whether anything local fits your situation.
steps: Contact a local animal shelter or humane organization and ask about temporary care for an owned pet during a planned hospital stay or recovery.
Ask about eligibility, notice, space, duration and costs. Make clear that you are asking about temporary care, not giving up your pet.
If a program fits, ask about its written owner-caregiver agreement and return arrangements. If not, request a specific local referral.
tasks.done_when: You understand a local program's suitability and next step, or have an honest answer that this route is unavailable.
tasks.use_when: She has a pet, explicitly expects an extended absence and lacks affordable care. Local research is required; no nationwide availability promise.
tasks.skip_when: Routine short sick-day planning, no pet, or a suitable carer already exists.
tasks.new_value: Discover a possible community alternative to commercial boarding without assuming it exists or confusing fostering with surrender.
tasks.cost: Inquiry free; program eligibility, fees and capacity vary.
tasks.waiting: Local organization reply; an inquiry never establishes a placement.

tasks.title: Help the care team understand your home situation
tasks.summary: If a hospital stay or procedure is planned, the team needs to know when there isn't someone at home to do the practical parts.
steps: Ask your procedure or hospital team who handles planning for help at home. Explain that you live alone and what help is actually available.
Discuss the daily activities you're unsure you could manage. Ask which need professional support and which could use ordinary practical help.
Request help coordinating the necessary arrangements, including costs and timing. Ask the team to confirm the plan before relying on it.
tasks.done_when: You and the care team have an agreed support plan, with unresolved arrangements clearly assigned for follow-up.
tasks.use_when: A hospital stay or procedure is explicitly planned and help at home is uncertain.
tasks.skip_when: Ordinary sick-day preparation with no planned treatment. A cleaner or errand helper must not be substituted for clinical/personal care.
tasks.new_value: Discover discharge or care-coordination support and explain the real home situation before a care plan assumes an available helper.
tasks.cost: Ask about coordination and service costs; eligibility and coverage vary.
tasks.waiting: Team coordination; 25 minutes is active discussion/preparation, not total arrangement time.
